title: The bond continues
hook: many keep a bond with the dead, and grief researchers now see it as healthy

segments.voice: Yesterday, grief that rises and falls instead of climbing stages. Your line was in waves. Did one come, and pass? Day eight hundred.

A phone, a name in the contacts, and a message sent anyway: got the job. wish you could see. Nobody will answer. She knows that. She sends it anyway, and puts the phone down, and feels a little less alone with the news. Somewhere else a man sets out his father's chair at the holiday table. A woman tells a gravestone about the new baby. For a long time, some schools of psychology would have called all of this a problem, a sign of grief not finished. Today, what changed, and what some traditions were doing all along.
screen: `A TEXT TO A NUMBER THAT WON'T ANSWER.` → `A CHAIR AT THE TABLE.` → `A PROBLEM, OR A BOND?`

segments.voice: First, the older view. In it, healthy grief meant letting go: slowly loosening your ties to the person who died, so your heart was free to attach elsewhere. Some trace the idea to Freud's essay Mourning and Melancholia. Keeping up a relationship with the dead could look like refusing to accept the death. Second, the turn. The researchers Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman gathered studies of grieving people in a book called Continuing Bonds. What they found was that people kept a relationship with their dead: talking to them, asking what they would think, carrying their values, feeling them near at a wedding. And that this was often part of healthy grieving, not a failure of it. Researchers since have added a fair caution: some bonds comfort and some trouble, depending on the person and the loss. Third, traditions had words for this already. In Jewish custom, after naming someone who has died, people add a short phrase: may their memory be a blessing. In some Japanese Buddhist homes, a household altar called a butsudan holds photos and memorial tablets, and family members greet the dead there, offer rice or tea, and tell them the news. Fourth, what continues is not the same as what was. The bond changes shape: from a voice on the phone to a voice in memory, from advice given to advice imagined, from a hand held to a value carried. The relationship moves. It doesn't have to end. The bond continues.
screen: `LET GO, SAID AN OLDER VIEW` · `CONTINUING BONDS` · `MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING` · `THE BOND CHANGES SHAPE` · then, large: `THE BOND CONTINUES.`

segments.voice: Choose someone who has died: a person, or even an animal. If no one comes, choose an ancestor you never met. Settle, and let them come to mind as they were on an ordinary day. Then, silently or under your breath, tell them one thing: a piece of news, a thank-you, a question. After that, simply sit, the way you would after saying something to a friend across the table. No answer is needed. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
The bond continues: a relationship with someone who has died that changes shape instead of ending. Today's word.
Your line: the bond continues. Today, do one small thing the person you spoke to would have liked, and let it count as staying in touch. Day eight hundred.

howItsDone: People keep bonds with the dead in many ways: Jewish families add "may their memory be a blessing" after a name, some Japanese Buddhist households greet the dead at a home altar, and others visit graves, keep a photo, or talk to the person on a walk.
